headline: WHEAT BREAKS 3.4%; SEPTEMBER WASDE COUNTDOWN BEGINS
subheadline: Friday's pre-holiday profit-taking hit wheat hardest while corn and beans drifted; the September 11 WASDE is the week's make-or-break event.
lead: Wheat closed $7.16, down 3.4% Friday, the biggest single-session drop in the complex. Corn drifted to $5.12 on light volume as Labor Day weekend stripped the room. Beans held better at $12.94, off just 1.1%. The whole week telegraphs one thing: the funds took profits before the holiday and are waiting for Thursday's export sales and Friday's WASDE to decide their next move.
the_takeaway: Wait through Labor Day; Thursday export sales and Friday's WASDE set the direction.
teaser: Wheat got hit hardest Friday; here's what the September 11 WASDE needs to show to matter.

one_number.unit: year-over-year rise in US LNG exports, H1 2026
one_number.context: US LNG exports averaged 17.4 Bcf/day in the first half of 2026, up 23% from a year ago per EIA. That export pace tightens domestic natural gas supply and puts a floor under natgas prices heading into fall fieldwork and harvest season.

yesterdays_call.summary: Called wheat lower through $7.00 on Friday's session.
yesterdays_call.note: Didn't play out. Wheat closed $7.16 -- down 3.4% on the day but never tested $7.00. The pre-holiday profit-taking moved the direction right but not the magnitude; the $7.00 level is still live and worth watching into Thursday's export sales.

sections.title: WHEAT BREAKS; GRAINS DRIFT
sections.body:
- Chicago wheat closed at **$7.16**, down 3.4% Friday, its biggest single-session drop in weeks; the AgWeb recap ties the pressure to pre-holiday profit-taking compounded by Black Sea peace-talk headlines that hit the geopolitical risk premium hard.
- Corn at $5.12 and December at $5.37 slipped 3.5 cents apiece, orderly and low-volume, consistent with a room that was already half-empty before the weekend.
- Soybeans at $12.94 held better than corn or wheat; meal at $345.30 closed at the top of its 52-week range, which is the one number telling you demand didn't walk away.
sections.catalyst: Pre-holiday profit-taking plus Black Sea peace-talk headlines deflated wheat's geopolitical risk premium.
sections.bottom_line: Wheat is the question mark this week; corn and beans are waiting for Friday's WASDE to move.
sections.vs_yesterday: Wheat: third straight session of heavy selling; narrative intact.

sections.title: CATTLE QUIET; TRUMP ORDERS MOVE
sections.body:
- Live cattle closed at $213.15, down just 0.5% Friday; feeders at $325.20 slipped 0.2%, both well above the screwworm-driven feeder rally lows, with the Aug 24 Douglas, AZ phased reopening of Mexican feeder imports now in the rearview.
- Trump signed two executive orders Friday supporting US ranchers and expanding market access for meat producers, per the Fence Post; no price mechanism yet, but the signal matters for packer concentration policy.
- The Cargill multi-plant lockout, ongoing since May 19, still removes roughly 6,000 head of daily processing capacity; packer margins, not cattle numbers, remain the binding constraint on the board.
sections.catalyst: Trump executive orders on rancher support signed Friday; Cargill lockout capacity constraint persists.
sections.bottom_line: Cattle are range-bound at low 52-week range territory; the executive orders are policy noise until they have teeth.

sections.title: ENERGY AND INPUTS INTO HARVEST
sections.body:
- WTI crude closed at $91.22, off 0.9% Friday; the Iran-Hormuz cycle, a July re-escalation that has since cooled, is back in the headlines as oilprice.com reports oil exporters are rushing to diversify channels and prices booked another weekly gain.
- Crack spreads remain elevated per EIA's Friday release; diesel tightness, not crude, is the harvest input-cost story, and AgWeb noted record-high diesel prices are already negating the margin benefit of $5-plus corn for some operations.
- Natural gas at $2.94 ticked up 0.7%, sitting at just 9% of its 52-week range; the LNG export pace covered in today's number is one reason the floor holds.
sections.catalyst: EIA confirmed elevated crack spreads Friday; Iran-Hormuz re-escalation keeping crude bids firm.
sections.bottom_line: Lock fall diesel if you haven't; the crack-spread data says the rack-price discount window is not getting wider.
sections.farmer_action: If you have unpriced fall diesel needs, the EIA crack-spread data says the current rack price is not the top of the range.

outside_the_pit.title: EPA and Army Seek More Input on WOTUS Definition
outside_the_pit.body: EPA and the Army Corps opened a supplemental comment period on the Waters of the US rule Friday, per Feedstuffs. Producers with tile-drained fields or seasonal wetlands should watch this closely; the final definition sets the scope of federal permits required for field drainage work.

outside_the_pit.title: CPKC Rail Reports Record Crop-Year Start for Grain Shipments
outside_the_pit.body: CPKC reported a record start to the 2026 crop year for grain movements, per World Grain. Strong rail capacity out of the Northern Plains heading into harvest is a logistics tailwind that can widen basis if it holds; watch whether the pace sustains once corn harvest volume accelerates.

the_more_you_know.title: Black Sea peace talks: the wheat premium that vanished in a day
the_more_you_know.body: Wheat's 3.4% drop Friday wasn't just profit-taking; it was a risk-premium unwind. When geopolitical tension in the Black Sea region eases even slightly, the supply-disruption insurance that traders pay above fundamental value drains fast. At $7.16, wheat is still 79% from its 52-week low; the floor is fundamentals, not fear.

watch_list.desc: USDA Weekly Export Sales. Wheat below 300K MT keeps the bear case alive after Friday's break; beans above 900K MT would support the meal-leads-oil thesis.
USDA Drought Monitor update. Any expansion into the eastern Corn Belt heading into harvest adds a yield-drag story the September WASDE may not have fully priced.

September WASDE. Corn yield above 181 bu/acre and beans above 53 bu/acre would push back against August's cuts and pressure the board; below August's 180.7/52.7 and December corn above $5.37 gets tested for a new leg.
USDA Crop Progress. First corn harvest percentage of the season; watch for early harvest pace vs the 5-year average as harvest pressure on basis begins.

daily_quote.text: Far more money has been lost by investors preparing for corrections than has been lost in corrections themselves.
